title: They differ in words but agree in substance
source_text: XXII. Proinde quum isti quidem asserunt eum quem Deus movet ad actum hunc, aut illum necessario agere; alii vero pertendunt nulla proprie dicta necessitate illum ad agendum impelli, verbis quidem discrepant, idem autem reipsa sentiunt. Nempe priores dicunt ejusmodi hominem necessario agere, quia impossibile est actum ejus a divina motione sejungi, quod alii non negant. Juxta posteriores autem nulla proprie dicta necessitate ad agendum tenetur, quia cum ipso ejus actu, ac proinde multo magis cum motione ad actum, optime consistit potestas ad actum contrarium, vel saltem ad actus istius carentiam, quod priores facile concedent.
pass_a_gloss: Accordingly when these indeed assert that he whom God moves to this, or that act acts necessarily; but others contend that he is impelled to acting by no necessity properly so called, they differ indeed in words, but think the same in fact. Namely the former say that a man of this kind acts necessarily, because it is impossible that his act be separated from the divine motion, which the others do not deny. But according to the latter he is held to acting by no necessity properly so called, because with his very act, and accordingly much more with the motion to the act, there very well consists a power to the contrary act, or at least to the lack of that act, which the former will readily grant.
pass_b_english: So when one party says that a man whom God moves to a given act acts necessarily, and the other insists that no necessity in the proper sense drives him to act, their words differ but their meaning is the same.

The first party says such a man acts necessarily because his act cannot be separated from God's motion, and the second does not deny it. The second says he is bound to act by no necessity in the proper sense, because a power to the opposite act, or at least to leaving the act undone, sits perfectly well with the act itself and still more with the motion toward it, and the first party readily grants that.

lemmas.latin: verbis quidem discrepant, idem autem reipsa sentiunt
lemmas.gloss: they differ in words, but think the same in fact

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.
